items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: there’s nobody in the world can play it like Sweets Edison and Buck Clayton

ctx.x: Well you know I never tried to play that style of music — Buck Clayton, Sweets Edison and the rest of them — because that’s the western band from Bennie Moten’s band. That band started out playing blues, that’s the way it was. Then later on through the years it started swinging, and still with the blues accent. And I was never a blues trumpet player. If I have to play it I’ll play it. But everything they had was swing and jump. And I was offered a job with Basie. He asked me one time he came and heard me play and…

say no one can play like Bird — they are in a class with Louis Armstrong. And you can’t kid yourself you know. I’m not going to jump in a band like that. So the Countsmen were never successful. They had Earle Warren leading and he was taking the lead, and he was leading the band. And he wasn’t in Count Basie’s band as the leader, see? But he couldn’t make it. He’s too loud and he was excited and he got upset all the time at things, and you can’t do that. So I’m just playing and I thank God for whatever I’m able…

items.title: 67246_Buck Clayton oral history interview
items.q: There are people like Doc Cheatham and Money Johnson.

ctx.x: I know. Snookey is a good man.
There are people like Doc Cheatham and Money Johnson. But there are very few left. Pat Jenkins.

Yes, I know. Yes, it gets scarce. Very scarce. People like Emmett Berry, Charlie Shavers. Some of them it just didn't seem to me that they are still not here. You know, like as healthy as Red Allen was at the Metropole and as good natured, a good kind of guy he was it just doesn't seem like things like that could happen, but they do. items.title: 54270_Doc Cheatham oral history interview
items.q: they sent me to Nancy, to play in Buck's place

ctx.x: Yes, because I had one of the saxophone players, I met, very fine -- on that engagement that I made played in Nancy, France, for Buck Clayton, Buck had two engagements the same night, one in Nancy and one somewhere else, so that was so many tickets sold, that they sent me to Nancy, to play in Buck's place, and that place was packed, I never saw a place like that, Buck played somewhere else. The manager he was biting his fingernails, he was worried, running (unin-)

looking at around (unintelligible) me, and running around, I don't know what he was talking about, and the musicians all seemed, they were -- they left, in fact they were in one part of the place louder than the other, they didn't socialize with me at all. Even on the train up, there -- one would come and say do you know "Royal Garden Blues?" I say I forgot the "Royal Garden Blues, man, I said, I've been playing it all my life and somebody asked me, do you know this, I says, look, don't worry about the concert,…
